title: No, not, not yet, there isn't
goal: Saying "no" correctly — four words for a job English splits between "no", "not" and "there isn't".
bekal: use *хэн ч*, *юу ч*, *хаана ч* for "nobody, nothing, nowhere"

dialogs.title: Яриа — Юу ч болоогүй
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for his lost room key. Sarnai helps him search, asking questions as they go.

notes: ⚠️ **Here is the full map — read this before any of the tables:** *биш* negates **nouns and adjectives**; *-гүй* attaches to **verbs**; *үгүй* stands alone as an **answer**; *байхгүй* means **"there isn't"**. Four words, four places, never swapped.

**Ч after a question word turns it into "-ever / even".** *Хаана* (where) → *хаана ч* (anywhere); *хэн* (who) → *хэн ч* (anyone). Paired with a negative, you get "nowhere", "nobody". ⚠️ The sentence **must** be negative — *хэн ч ирсэн* without a negative means nothing.

**The -аагүй / -ээгүй form means "not yet", a subtle step away from -сангүй, which means "didn't".** *Яваагүй* = hasn't gone (maybe later); *явсангүй* = didn't go after all. In conversation, *-аагүй* is far more common — use it when unsure.
**Л means "just, only" and sits right after the word it limits.** *Гэртээ **л** байсан* = was just at home. This tiny word is everywhere and instantly makes you sound natural.

**Чамгүйгээр = "without you".** Notice three suffixes stacked: *чам* (you) + *-гүй* (without) + *-гээр* (with). Mongolian stacks suffixes freely, always in a fixed order. You don't need to copy this yet, but learn to recognize it when you hear it.

grammars.title: The four negators and where each one goes
body: This table is the heart of the unit. Read the last column alongside it — English also splits "no", "not" and "there isn't", just along slightly different lines.
after: ⚠️ The last row shows a different and very productive use of *-гүй*: attached to a **noun**, it means "without" and builds a new adjective, much like English "-less". *Цаг**гүй*** (no time), *ажил**гүй*** (unemployed), *асуудал**гүй*** (no problem), *хамаа**гүй*** (doesn't matter, whatever).

**Its partner is -тай, which you met in unit 3.** *Мөнгө**тэй*** (with money) versus *мөнгө**гүй*** (without money). These two suffixes work as a pair and together build a large share of Mongolian adjectives.

grammars.title: Negating verbs in every tense
body: The negative suffix changes with the tense. Read this table aloud line by line, comparing the second and third columns.
after: **The pattern in one sentence: take the dictionary form (ending in -х) and add -гүй.** *Явах* → *явахгүй*; *мэдэх* → *мэдэхгүй*; *ойлгох* → *ойлгохгүй*. That is the present/future negative, and it covers most of what you need.

⚠️ For habits, two suffixes stack: *явдаг* + *-гүй* = *явдаггүй*, with **two г in a row**. It looks odd but is correct, and it comes up often: *иддэггүй* (doesn't eat), *уудаггүй* (doesn't drink), *ярьдаггүй* (doesn't talk).

sections.title: Question word + ч = nothing at all

head: Form
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: *Хаана ч байхгүй.* — It's nowhere to be found.
*Ямар ч асуудалгүй.* — No problem at all.
*Хэд ч байхгүй.* — There isn't a single one.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **The sentence must be negative.** This rule is absolute: *хэн ч* always pairs with *байхгүй*, *-гүй* or *-аагүй*. Mongolian uses **double negatives**, just like Russian or casual "I ain't seen nobody" — something standard English calls wrong.

blocks.title: Without a negative, the meaning flips
items: *Хэн ч ирж болно.* — **Anyone** can come. (Positive, so it means "everyone".)
*Хаана ч явж болно.* — You can go **anywhere**.
⚠️ So *ч* itself is neutral: the negative decides the meaning. Just like English "anyone", which means "everyone" in "anyone can come" but "no one" in "I didn't see anyone".

blocks.text: **This pattern is one of the most useful tools in Mongolian**, because it turns any noun into an adjective with no new words to memorize. If you know *хүч* (strength), you automatically know *хүчтэй* (strong) and *хүчгүй* (weak). If you know *ус* (water), you know *устай* (watery) and *усгүй* (dry).

blocks.title: The four negative sentences you'll need most

blocks.text: This point **trips up English speakers**, because Mongolian answers negative questions the opposite way from English.

⚠️ Notice that *тийм* (yes) here means **"right, you guessed correctly"** — not "yes, I'm going". Asked "aren't you going?", *тийм* means "right, I'm not". English works the other way round, so this is a spot where you have to **consciously flip your instinct.**
